poissons.resume: What you are allowed to fish, what you can eat, what you must release, and the real dangers: pollution, parasites, spines and venom.

p: In Wallonia as in France, fishing requires a licence, and each species has its seasons, minimum sizes and sometimes quotas. Some species must always be released: eel, salmon, and protected species such as bullhead or the noble crayfish. The sheet “Fishing: what the law says” summarises the rules.

encadre.texte: If in doubt about a species or a rule: release it. A fish put back costs you nothing, a protected species taken can cost a lot.

sections.titre: Eat or release: the three groups
liste: Good to eat, within the rules: trout, perch, zander, roach, chub, pike (watch the bones and teeth).
Eat with caution: large bottom-feeders and old predators (carp, catfish, barbel, big pike), which concentrate pollutants. Barbel roe is poisonous.
Always release: eel, salmon, grayling, bullhead, noble crayfish.
Invasive species (signal crayfish, black bullhead) can be eaten, but must never be transported alive.

p: PCBs, dioxins, mercury and PFAS can't be seen or smelled and don't disappear with cooking. They build up in fish fat over the years. Simple rule: small, young, lean and caught upstream, away from towns. Never eel. Remove skin and fat.

encadre.texte: Never eat a fish found dead or a fish caught in an area where a ban on taking fish is posted.

p: Some freshwater fish (pike, perch, coarse fish) can carry parasitic worms transmissible to humans, such as the fish tapeworm. Thorough cooking destroys them: the flesh must be opaque and come away from the bone. No tartare, no ceviche, no barely seared river fish.

liste: Perch and zander: dorsal spines. Fold the fin down before grabbing the fish.
Pike: very sharp teeth. Never put your fingers in its mouth.
Catfish (bullhead): hard spines and a very painful sting.
In the North Sea and the Atlantic, the weever hides in the sand; in the Mediterranean, the scorpionfish: venomous spines. The venom is treated with very hot water.

p: An improvised line (pin, thorn, gorge hook) and bait found under stones can feed you. But fishing is slow and uncertain: a healthy adult lasts weeks without eating, only a few days without water, and only a few hours if very cold. The priorities remain shelter, water, fire and signalling.

cuisine.resume: Cooking on a stove or on embers, without utensils, and a few recipes with foraged food.

p: A stove (gas, alcohol, wood) is quick, clean and allowed where fires are not. It remains the main bivouac tool. A wood fire is for designated places or emergencies.
With a stove: always cook outside or under a well-ventilated porch, never in the tent (fire and carbon monoxide), on flat, stable ground, protected from the wind by a windshield.

liste: Cook on the embers, not the flames: they heat evenly and don't blacken everything.
For the pot: rest it on two big parallel logs or two dry stones, or hang it from a tripod.
Never use river stones near the fire: the water they contain can make them burst.
Never skewer food with yew, oleander or cherry laurel wood (poisonous).
In a parcel: wrap the food in aluminium foil (or large edible leaves, such as lime), and put it in the embers.
On a flat stone: a dry, flat stone heated at the edge of the fire works as a griddle.
On a spit: on a fresh hazel branch, above the embers.
In the ashes: scored chestnuts, potatoes and apples cook straight in the embers.
Nettle soup: young leaves picked with gloves, boiled for 10 minutes with a stock cube and a few instant mash flakes.
Embers-roasted chestnuts: score each chestnut with a cross, 15 to 20 minutes in the embers, turning them.
Pine tea: a handful of chopped pine needles steeped for 10 minutes (beware of yew).
Rose hip tea: fruits opened and cleared of their hairs, boiled and then carefully strained through a cloth.
Wild garlic pesto: leaves identified one by one, crushed with oil, salt and hazelnuts.

encadre.texte: Every wild ingredient must have been identified with certainty. If in doubt about a single leaf, throw everything away.

liste: Wash your hands before cooking (hand gel or soapy water away from the river).
Boil the water for cooking and washing up.
Wash up more than 50 m from water, and strain the washing-up water before scattering it.
Take all leftovers away: they attract animals.

sections.titre: Campfire recipes inspired by video games
p: Skewers, stews, honey apples: many adventure games have their heroes cook on a campfire. These recipes are real-life versions, doable on a bivouac with a mess tin, a green branch and good embers. Each sheet lists the “loot” to bring, the cooking and a small tongue-in-cheek effect.

encadre.texte: Original recipes written for Bivaska. The games mentioned are inspirations: Bivaska is neither affiliated with nor endorsed by their publishers.

orientation_guide.resume: Map and compass, natural methods, and what to do when you're lost.

liste: North is at the top of the map.
Scale: on a 1:25,000 map, 1 cm represents 250 m. It's the ideal scale for hiking.
Contour lines join points of the same altitude: close together, the slope is steep; far apart, the ground is flat.
Orient the map: turn it so that what you see in front of you is in front of you on the map.

etapes: Put the compass on the map, its edge joining your position to your destination.
Turn the dial until the dial's north-south lines are parallel to the map's north-south lines, arrow pointing north.
Hold the compass flat in front of you and turn on the spot until the red needle sits inside the dial's arrow.
The direction-of-travel arrow now shows the way. Aim at a distant landmark in that direction (tree, rock), walk to it, and repeat.

encadre.texte: In Western Europe, the difference between magnetic north and true north is now very small: you can ignore it when hiking.

liste: The sun rises in the east, is due south around midday and sets in the west.
The stick-and-shadow method gives the east-west line in 15 minutes.
An analogue watch gives south in good weather.
The North Star gives north at night.
Moss growing “on the north side” of trees is NOT reliable: it grows mainly on the damp side, which varies with the terrain.
Count your steps: most adults take 60 to 70 double steps per 100 m. Calibrate yourself before you go.
Cross-bearing: two compass bearings on two known landmarks give your exact position on the map.
Handrail: follow a linear feature (path, river, forest edge) rather than cutting through the woods.
Aiming off: deliberately aim to one side of the target so you know which way to turn when you arrive.
Catching feature: a feature beyond your goal that tells you you've gone too far.
The phone's GPS position works without a network: only the map must have been loaded beforehand (in Bivaska, by browsing the area).
Accuracy drops under dense forest cover, at the bottom of gorges and near cliffs: you can be off by several dozen metres.
Cold and GPS drain the battery quickly: keep the phone warm, in aeroplane mode, and carry a power bank.
GPS tells you where you are, not which way to go: a map, a compass and the habit of reading the terrain remain essential.

etapes: Stop (STOP method): walking on at random almost always makes things worse.
Look at your GPS position in Bivaska: it works without a network, and the map stays visible if the area was displayed before.
Go back to the last place you knew for certain, if it's possible and close.
Otherwise, look for a handrail: a path, a river to follow downstream, a power line, a ridge.
If night is coming, stop, build a shelter and signal: you'll set off again in daylight.

encadre.texte: If someone knows where you are, staying put is almost always safer than wandering.

deplacement.resume: Walking pace, difficult terrain, walking at night and crossing streams.

liste: Walk at a pace where you can still talk: if you're out of breath, you sweat and wear yourself out.
A short break every hour to drink, eat a little and check your feet.
In a group, the slowest walks in front and sets the pace.
Count about 4 km an hour on a flat path, much less in forest, uphill or with a heavy pack. Add an hour for every 300 to 400 m of climb.
Downhill: small steps, knees slightly bent, poles in front. Most sprains happen going down, when tired.
Slippery ground (roots, wet rocks, leaves): put your foot down flat, never on a slanting root.
Dense vegetation: go round rather than force through, protect your eyes from branches, keep one hand free.
Scree and steep slopes: one at a time, never one person above another.

p: At night, speed halves and the risk of a fall or a navigation error soars. Only walk at night on a known path, head torch on, with spare batteries. Otherwise, the safest thing is to stop, build a shelter and set off again at daybreak.
This is one of the most dangerous situations when hiking. A current reaching the knees is enough to knock an adult over.
etapes: First ask yourself whether you can avoid it: a bridge further on, a detour, waiting for the level to drop (in the morning, after a storm).
Choose the spot: wide, shallow, split into several channels, without slippery rocks, upstream of a sandbank.
Keep your shoes on, undo the pack's straps.
Cross facing the current, leaning on a stick on the upstream side, angling downstream.
In a group, stand shoulder to shoulder, the strongest upstream.

encadre.texte: Never above a waterfall or rapids, never in very cold water or a flood. If you fall: on your back, feet first at the surface, swim diagonally towards the bank.

meteo_dangers.resume: Thunderstorms, cold, heat, fog, floods and wind: anticipate and react.

p: Lightning is one of the great dangers of mountains and wide open spaces. Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder: under 30 seconds, the storm is less than 10 km away and you should already be under shelter. Then wait 30 minutes after the last thunderclap before setting off again.
liste: Leave summits, ridges, isolated trees, cable lines and water (lake, river).
In a forest: stand among trees of the same height, in a hollow, away from the tallest trees.
Move away from metal objects (poles, pylons, fences).
If caught in the open: crouch, feet together, on your pack or mat, head tucked in, without lying down.
In a group: spread out several metres apart so a single strike doesn't hit everyone.

encadre.texte: A tent or a shallow cave doesn't protect you from lightning. A closed car does.

p: You can get hypothermia at +10 °C, in rain and wind. The signs progress: shivering, clumsy movements, then confusion and drowsiness. Someone who stops shivering while still cold is in great danger.
liste: Shelter the casualty from wind and rain, insulate them from the ground.
Replace wet clothes with dry ones, cover the head.
Give hot, sweet drinks if they are conscious.
Warm gently: skin-to-skin contact in the sleeping bag, wrapped hot-water bottles on the trunk (not the limbs).
Call 112 as soon as there is confusion or drowsiness.
Set off early, take your break during the hot hours, in the shade.
Drink regularly before you feel thirsty, and eat salty food.
Signs of heatstroke: hot skin, headache, nausea, confusion. Move to the shade, cool down with water on the skin and by fanning, call 112 if there is confusion.
Fog makes you lose your bearings in minutes: stop, follow a known path or the compass, stay together.
At night, move slowly, head torch on, and don't leave the paths. Better to bivouac than to walk in the dark on unknown ground.
Never camp in a riverbed, on a gravel bar or right by the water: the level can rise very quickly after a storm upstream.
Never cross a river in flood or whose water is above the knees.
In strong wind (gusts over 60 km/h, alerts in the Bivouac tab): avoid the forest and never sleep under trees.
